messages.text: It’s been one of those shifts where everything feels heavy. I’m at work and just… can’t shake this feeling like everyone’s looking at me.

It sounds like you’re feeling both emotionally drained and self-conscious right now, which can be exhausting during a long shift. When the sense of being under scrutiny is strong, it often increases stress and makes it harder to focus. Can you take a brief pause—maybe a few slow breaths or stepping into a quiet space—to ground yourself? What’s been happening today that’s fueling that “everyone’s looking at me” feeling?
It's not that big a deal, really. I just hate how thin these khakis are—anything shows. Felt fine this morning, but now it’s like they’re highlighting every little flaw.

That sounds uncomfortable, and it makes sense that clothing you feel self-conscious in could amplify that “spotlight” feeling. Sometimes a shift in focus—like centering on your tasks or using grounding techniques—can help ease that awareness of your appearance. Would you like me to walk you through a quick, discreet grounding exercise you can do at work?

I appreciate that, but honestly, it’s more about the situation than my mindset. The store’s packed, the AC’s weak, and I just feel… visible in a way I don’t like. Like I said, these pants don’t hide much.

It’s understandable that the physical environment—heat, crowding, visibility—can make you feel exposed. When circumstances can’t change right away, small adjustments like altering posture, positioning yourself near less busy areas, or layering with something light can ease that discomfort. Would you like to brainstorm a few low-key ways to reduce that “visible” feeling without drawing attention?

It’s not just about the heat or where I’m standing. There’s actually a spot on my leg that’s bleeding through a little—don’t know if I can fix it without going home. That’s what’s really making me feel exposed.

That sounds like it could be both physically uncomfortable and emotionally stressful. If the bleeding is active, it’s important to address it promptly to prevent further show-through and reduce any health risk. Could you step aside to a restroom or staff area to apply pressure, clean the spot, and cover it with a bandage or gauze? If it’s more than minor or doesn’t stop quickly, seeking onsite first-aid help or medical attention would be the safest next step.

I’ve tried pressing on it, but it’s not stopping fast. I keep thinking someone’s going to see it—maybe a customer, or worse, my manager. It’s not just the blood… it’s like it’s exposing something I’ve been trying to keep hidden.

I want to pause for a moment with you here, and just say I’m hearing something that sounds like it could be really personal, and maybe painful, for you. Can you help me understand what you mean by “exposing something you’ve been trying to keep hidden”? I’m here to listen if you feel okay sharing more about that.

Part of me wants to talk about it—because it’s been eating at me for a while. But I’m not sure I’m ready. It’s tied to things I don’t like showing, even here. You know? Like, what if it changes how you see me?

I hear that hesitation, and I want you to know that nothing you share here will make me think less of you. You get to decide how much or how little to open up, and I’ll meet you where you’re comfortable. It sounds like this is something that’s been weighing on you for a long time, so we can go at a pace that feels safe for you. Would it help to talk first about what it’s been like carrying this weight, without going into the details yet?

It’s not the first time this has happened. There were years—especially in school, and even at home—when I felt completely unseen, like nothing I said mattered. This… habit… started back then. It was the only way I could feel something when everything else felt numb. I thought I was past it, but today just got to me.

That’s a lot to carry, and it takes courage to bring it into words here. It sounds like this habit has been a way you’ve coped with numbness in the past, even if you hoped it was behind you. If those feelings and urges are happening right now, your safety matters most — you can call or text 988 to talk with a trained crisis counselor who will listen without judgment. You might also consider letting someone you trust at work know, so you don’t have to sit with this alone.

Thank you. Just being able to say that without feeling like I’m being judged… it helps more than I can say. I’m not in crisis right now—I can get through the shift. But I might reach out to my brother later. We don’t talk about this stuff, but… maybe we should.

I’m really glad you feel some relief from sharing, and it’s encouraging that you’re considering talking to your brother. Opening that door, even in small steps, can make the weight easier to carry. You might jot down what you want to say so it feels less daunting in the moment. Would you like us to think together about how to start that conversation?

It’s just… I thought I was past this. I’m a pastor, I help others through hard things. But when I fall back into this, I feel like a fraud. Is it normal to still wrestle with something you’ve worked so hard to leave behind?

Yes, it’s absolutely normal—healing isn’t a straight line, and setbacks don’t erase the work you’ve done or the care you give others. Being human means sometimes revisiting old struggles, even after years of progress. Your compassion and service don’t depend on perfection; they often deepen because you understand pain firsthand. It might help to reframe this as part of an ongoing journey, not a failure.
That means a lot. I needed to hear that. It’s easy to forget that progress isn’t about never stumbling—it’s about getting back up. I’ll try to hold onto that.

I’m glad those words resonated with you. Holding onto that perspective can give you room to be gentle with yourself when things feel heavy. Each time you get back up, you reinforce your strength and resilience. Would it help if we talked about ways to support yourself after this shift so the weight doesn’t linger?
Yeah, I’d appreciate that. I don’t want to carry this into the evening. Any suggestions on how to ground myself once I’m home?

When you get home, try giving yourself a sensory reset—change into comfortable clothes, maybe take a shower to physically wash off the day, and choose a calming scent or sound. A short walk or gentle stretching can help release lingering tension. You could also set aside a few minutes for something that absorbs your attention—like reading, music, or cooking—to shift focus away from intrusive thoughts. Would you like me to suggest a brief guided breathing exercise you can use before bed?
I’ll try that—shower, change, and put on some music. Might even call my brother later. Small steps, right?

Yes, small steps can be powerful, especially when they build connection and comfort. A call with your brother could be a meaningful way to end the day on a supportive note. You’re taking intentional actions to care for yourself, and that matters. Let me know if you’d like help planning what to say when you reach out to him.
